draft.title: Juries
card: A jury is a group of ordinary citizens who decide the facts in a criminal trial. In Victoria, a jury of 12 is used in serious (indictable) trials in the County Court and the Supreme Court.
The jury decides whether the accused is guilty or not guilty. The judge directs the jury on the law and runs the trial, but the jury decides guilt.
A jury is first asked to reach a unanimous verdict, where all 12 agree. In some cases, after long deliberation, a majority verdict may be accepted instead.

Under the Juries Act 2000 (Vic), a verdict of 11 to 1 may be accepted only after at least six hours of deliberation. It is not available for murder, treason and certain serious Commonwealth drug offences, which need a unanimous verdict.
draft.remember: In Victoria, a jury of 12 decides guilt. An 11 to 1 verdict is allowed only after six hours, and never for murder.

a.q: In a Victorian County Court trial with a jury, who decides if the accused is guilty?
opts: The jury of 12 citizens
The judge who runs the trial
The prosecutor for the state
The defence lawyer for the accused
a.why: The jury decides the facts and reaches the verdict. The judge runs the trial and directs the jury on the law, which is why the judge is the most tempting wrong answer, but the judge does not decide guilt.
a.clue: Think about who weighs the evidence, not who runs the court.

b.q: A Victorian jury in an armed robbery trial has deliberated for over six hours and is split 11 to 1 for guilty. What can the judge do?
opts: Accept the 11 to 1 majority verdict
Order a retrial before a new jury
Enter a verdict of guilty without the jury
Direct the jury to stay until all 12 agree
b.why: Armed robbery allows a majority verdict in Victoria. After at least six hours of deliberation, the judge may accept 11 to 1. The same step would not be allowed in a murder trial, which needs a unanimous verdict.
b.clue: Six hours have passed and the offence allows a majority verdict.

problems.detail: The exclusions from majority verdicts are misstated. Under s 46 of the Juries Act 2000 (Vic), majority verdicts are not available for murder, treason, certain Victorian drug offences (trafficking or cultivating a large commercial quantity) and any Commonwealth offence. Commonwealth offences need unanimity under s 80 of the Constitution. The exclusion is not limited to 'certain serious Commonwealth drug offences'.
The clue gives the answer away by stating that the offence allows a majority verdict and that six hours have passed. Those are exactly the conditions for accepting an 11 to 1 verdict.

b.q: A Victorian jury in an armed robbery trial has deliberated for seven hours and is split 11 to 1 for guilty. Can the judge accept this verdict?
opts: Yes, as the time and offence allow a majority verdict
No, as every criminal verdict must be unanimous
No, as a majority verdict needs at least two days
No, as armed robbery is treated the same as murder
b.why: Armed robbery is not one of the excluded offences, and more than six hours have passed, so the judge may accept 11 to 1. The tempting wrong answer is that every verdict must be unanimous: a jury is asked for unanimity first, but a majority can be accepted for most offences.
b.clue: Compare this trial with the limits on majority verdicts.
